  "question_id": "d3905f6d3c31af4cdf5d47d3e6380179c5fd2c8f55e489648d140783b06a0d3b:p0014:l0011:question",
  "rule": "literal_source_boundaries_and_primary_options",
  "before": {
    "stem": "29. The court in this case justified application of Article 30(1) to educational institutions\nestablished by religious and linguistic minorities before commencement of Constitution\nthrough a co-joint reading of Article 30, with Articles 13 and 372. In doing so it observed\nthat ‘Article 13(1) has a retroactive effect and not a retrospective effect.’ Which of the\nfollowing statement best captures the difference between the two effects?",
    "options": [
      {
        "label": "A",
        "raw_label": "(A)",
        "text": "A provision is retrospective if it alters the position of law before its\nenactment/commencement, it is retroactive if it imposes new results for previous\nactions"
      },
      {
        "label": "B",
        "raw_label": "(B)",
        "text": "A retroactive effect applies only prospectively, whereas retrospective effect alters\npast rights and liabilities"
      },
      {
        "label": "C",
        "raw_label": "(C)",
        "text": "A provision is retrospective if it applies to past and closed transactions, whereas\nprovision is retroactive if it applies only to future cases"
      },
      {
        "label": "D",
        "raw_label": "(D)",
        "text": "A retrospective provision alters both substantive and procedural rights in the past,\nwhile a retroactive provision affects only substantive law"
      }
    ]
  },

    "stem": "31. d3905f6d3c31af4cdf5d47d3e6380179c5fd2c8f55e489648d140783b06a0d3b:p0016:l0013:question
{
  "question_id": "d3905f6d3c31af4cdf5d47d3e6380179c5fd2c8f55e489648d140783b06a0d3b:p0016:l0013:question",
  "rule": "literal_source_boundaries_and_primary_options",
  "before": {
    "stem": "34. Article 323A and 323B of the Indian Constitution for the establishment of tribunal to\nadjudicate disputes in specific matters. While both articles deal with tribunals, there are\nkey differences in their scope and application. Which of the following statements\ncorrectly reflect the distinction between Article 323A and 323B?",
    "options": [
      {
        "label": "A",
        "raw_label": "(A)",
        "text": "Article 323A exclusively deals with administrative tribunals for public service\nmatters, while Article 323B deals with the tribunals for a wider range of subjects\nincluding taxation and land reforms."
      },
      {
        "label": "B",
        "raw_label": "(B)",
        "text": "While tribunals under Article 323A can be established only by Parliament,\ntribunals under Article 323B can only be established by State legislature, with\nmatters falling within their legislative competence."
      },
      {
        "label": "C",
        "raw_label": "(C)",
        "text": "Under Article 323A, only one tribunal for centre and no tribunal for state may be\nestablished. As far as Article 323B is concerned, there is no hierarchy of tribunals."
      },
      {
        "label": "D",
        "raw_label": "(D)",
        "text": "Article 323A grant tribunals the power to hear appeals directly from the Supreme\nCourt, by passing the high court. Under Article 323B there is no such power."
      }
    ]
  },
  "after": {
    "stem": "34. Article 323A and 323B of the Indian Constitution for the establishment of tribunal to adjudicate disputes in specific matters.     "options": [

        "raw_label": "(A)",
        "text": "Article 323A exclusively deals with administrative tribunals for public service matters, while Article 323B deals with the tribunals for a wider range of subjects including taxation and land reforms."
      },
      {
        "label": "B",
        "raw_label": "(B)",
        "text": "While tribunals under Article 323A can be established only by Parliament, tribunals under Article 323B can only be established by State legislature, with matters falling within their legislative competence."
      },
      {
        "label": "C",
        "raw_label": "(C)",
        "text": "Under Article 323A, only one tribunal for centre and no tribunal for state may be established. As far as Article 323B is concerned, there is no hierarchy of tribunals."
      },
      {
        "label": "D",
        "raw_label": "(D)",
        "text": "Article 323A grant tribunals the power to hear appeals directly from the Supreme Court, by passing the high court. Under Article 323B there is no such power."
      }
    ]
  },

    "stem": "38. The main test to find out whether a document constitutes a ‘Will’ or a ‘Settlement’ is to\nsee whether the disposition of the interest in the property is in praesenti in favour of the\nsettlee or whether the disposition is to take effect on the death of the executant. In view\nof this position of law, choose the CORRECT proposition:",
    "options": [
      {
        "label": "A",
        "raw_label": "(A)",
        "text": "If the disposition is to take effect on the death of the executant, it will be a\nSettlement. But, if the executant divests his interest in the property and vests his\ninterest in praesenti in the transferee, the document will be a Will."
      },
      {
        "label": "B",
        "raw_label": "(B)",
        "text": "Whether the disposition is to take effect on the death of the executant or the\nexecutant divests his interest in the property and vests his interest in praesenti in\nthe transferee, the document will nevertheless remain a Settlement."
      },
      {
        "label": "C",
        "raw_label": "(C)",
        "text": "If the disposition is to take effect on the death of the executant, it will be a Will.\nBut, if the executant divests his interest in the property and vests his interest in\npraesenti in the settlee, the document will be a Settlement."
      },
      {
        "label": "D",
        "raw_label": "(D)",
        "text": "If the disposition takes effect on the assumption of death of the executant, it shall\nbe a will."
      }
    ]
  },

d3905f6d3c31af4cdf5d47d3e6380179c5fd2c8f55e489648d140783b06a0d3b:p0021:l0000:question
{
  "question_id": "d3905f6d3c31af4cdf5d47d3e6380179c5fd2c8f55e489648d140783b06a0d3b:p0021:l0000:question",
  "rule": "literal_source_boundaries_and_primary_options",
  "before": {
    "stem": "47. The bench in this case referred to a distinction drawn previously in Grindlays Bank case,\nthat of procedural review and substantive review by criminal courts. Which of the\nfollowing statements most accurately captures the distinction between the two decisions?",
    "options": [
      {
        "label": "A",
        "raw_label": "(A)",
        "text": "A procedural review is exercised when a higher court finds an error in\ninterpretation, while a substantive review is limited to correcting factual\ninaccuracies within the same court."
      },
      {
        "label": "B",
        "raw_label": "(B)",
        "text": "A procedural review is available only in appellate courts, whereas a substantive\nreview may be conducted by the original court that issued in court"
      },
      {
        "label": "C",
        "raw_label": "(C)",
        "text": "A procedural review is inherent or implied in a court to set aside a palpably\nerroneous order passed under misapprehension by it. However, a substantive\nreview is when error sought to be corrected is one of law and is apparent on the\nface of the record."
      },
      {
        "label": "D",
        "raw_label": "(D)",
        "text": "A procedural review involves correcting errors of judgement made after hearing the\nparties while a substantive review is confined to omissions in recording of legal\nreasoning."
      }
    ]
  },

  "before": {
    "stem": "53. What is the minimum essential ingredient that the Supreme Court found prima facie\ndisclosed in the complaint for an offence under Section 387 IPC?",
    "options": [

        "label": "A",
        "raw_label": "(A)",
        "text": "The transfer of at least Rs. 5 lakhs from the complainant to the accused."
      },

      },
      {
        "label": "C",
        "raw_label": "(C)",
        "text": "Putting the complainant in fear of death or grievous hurt in order to commit\nextortion, such as by pointing a gun and demanding Rs. 5 lakhs per month."
      },

        "label": "D",
        "raw_label": "(D)",
        "text": "The existence of pending litigation regarding Trademark and Copyright claims."

d3905f6d3c31af4cdf5d47d3e6380179c5fd2c8f55e489648d140783b06a0d3b:p0023:l0018:question
{
  "question_id": "d3905f6d3c31af4cdf5d47d3e6380179c5fd2c8f55e489648d140783b06a0d3b:p0023:l0018:question",
  "rule": "literal_source_boundaries_and_primary_options",
  "before": {
    "stem": "54. The Supreme Court cites which of the following as a well-settled principle of law\nregarding the interpretation of penal statutes?",
    "options": [
      {
        "label": "A",
        "raw_label": "(A)",
        "text": "Penal statutes must be given a wide and flexible interpretation to cover all\nintended mischief."
      },
      {
        "label": "B",
        "raw_label": "(B)",
        "text": "Courts are competent to stretch the meaning of an expression used by the\nLegislature to carry out the intention of the Legislature."
      },
      {
        "label": "C",
        "raw_label": "(C)",
        "text": "If two possible and reasonable constructions can be put upon a penal provision, the\nCourt must lean towards the construction that imposes the maximum penalty."
      },
      {
        "label": "D",
        "raw_label": "(D)",
        "text": "If two possible and reasonable constructions can be put upon a penal provision, the\nCourt must lean towards that construction which exempts the subject from penalty\nrather than the one which imposes penalty."
      }
    ]
  },

d3905f6d3c31af4cdf5d47d3e6380179c5fd2c8f55e489648d140783b06a0d3b:p0024:l0019:question
{
  "question_id": "d3905f6d3c31af4cdf5d47d3e6380179c5fd2c8f55e489648d140783b06a0d3b:p0024:l0019:question",
  "rule": "literal_source_boundaries_and_primary_options",
  "before": {
    "stem": "56. When a Hindu Mitakshara coparcener, who has a child legitimised under section 16 of\nHindu Marriage Act 1955, dies intestate, after the 2005 Amendment of the Hindu\nSuccession Act, 1956, what is the legal mechanism that determines the child’s share in\nthe parent’s interest in the coparcenary property?",
    "options": [
      {
        "label": "A",
        "raw_label": "(A)",
        "text": "The Child becomes a coparcener by birth, and the entire coparcenary property is\ndivided equally amongst all the coparceners."
      },
      {
        "label": "B",
        "raw_label": "(B)",
        "text": "The parent’s interest devolves by traditional rule of survivorship, and the section\n16 child receives no share"
      },
      {
        "label": "C",
        "raw_label": "(C)",
        "text": "The parent’s interest is first determined through a notional partition immediately\nbefore death under section 6 (3) of Hindu Succession Act 1956 and this determined\nshare then devolves by intestate succession to all the deceased’s children\n(including the section 16 child) under section 8/10 of Hindu Succession Act 1956."
      },
      {
        "label": "D",
        "raw_label": "(D)",
        "text": "The share of section 16 child is limited to receiving maintenance from the joint\nfamily estate."
      }
    ]
  },
  "after": {

    "stem": "65. Under Indian Law, can a woman in a live in relationship claim maintenance under S.\n125, CrPC despite not being a legally wedded wife?",

      {
        "label": "A",
        "raw_label": "(A)",
        "text": "No, as per the interpretation of statute ‘wife’ means legally wedded wife and\nincludes who has been divorced by, or has obtained a divorce from her husband."
      },
      {
        "label": "B",
        "raw_label": "(B)",
        "text": "Yes, a woman in a live in relationship can claim maintenance u/s 125, CrPC as\nstrict proof of marriage is not necessary and maintenance cannot be denied if\nevidence suggests cohabitation."
      },
      {
        "label": "C",
        "raw_label": "(C)",
        "text": "A woman in live in relationship can only claim maintenance if she has been\ncohabiting for more than five years and dependent children from the relationship."
      },
      {
        "label": "D",
        "raw_label": "(D)",
        "text": "A woman in live in relationship can claim maintenance only through a civil suit as\nthe protection of women from domestic violence act 2005 (PWDVA) does not apply\nto live in relationships."
      }
    ]

    "stem": "65. Under Indian Law, can a woman in a live in relationship claim maintenance under S. 125, CrPC despite not being a legally wedded wife?",
    "options": [
      {
        "label": "A",
        "raw_label": "(A)",
        "text": "No, as per the interpretation of statute ‘wife’ means legally wedded wife and includes who has been divorced by, or has obtained a divorce from her husband."
      },
      {
        "label": "B",
        "raw_label": "(B)",
        "text": "Yes, a woman in a live in relationship can claim maintenance u/s 125, CrPC as strict proof of marriage is not necessary and maintenance cannot be denied if evidence suggests cohabitation."
      },
      {
        "label": "C",
        "raw_label": "(C)",
        "text": "A woman in live in relationship can only claim maintenance if she has been cohabiting for more than five years and dependent children from the relationship."
      },
      {
        "label": "D",
        "raw_label": "(D)",
        "text": "A woman in live in relationship can claim maintenance only through a civil suit as the protection of women from domestic violence act 2005 (PWDVA) does not apply to live in relationships. 27 ρ PG 2026"
      }
    ]
  },

  "before": {

    "options": [
      {
        "label": "A",
        "raw_label": "(A)",
        "text": "Whether the assessee's claim for a long-term capital gain was correctly disallowed\nby the Assessing Officer."

        "text": "Whether the reduction in the number of shares due to a reduction in share capital\namounted to a \"transfer\" under Section 2(47) of the Income Tax Act, 1961, allowing\nfor a capital loss claim."

      {
        "label": "C",
        "raw_label": "(C)",
        "text": "Whether the High Court of Karnataka correctly relied on the decision of Anarkali\nSarabhai v. CIT."
      },
      {
        "label": "D",
        "raw_label": "(D)",
        "text": "Whether the face value of the shares remaining the same after the reduction\nnullified the claim of capital loss."
      }

    "stem": "67. According to the Supreme Court, why does a reduction in share capital that\nproportionately reduces a shareholder's rights amount to a \"transfer\" under Section 2(47)\nof the Income Tax Act, 1961?",
    "options": [
      {
        "label": "A",
        "raw_label": "(A)",
        "text": "Because the shareholder's voting percentage remains constant, which is a form of\ncontinuous transfer."
      },
      {
        "label": "B",
        "raw_label": "(B)",
        "text": "Because it involves a sale or exchange of the capital asset to another party."
      },
      {
        "label": "C",
        "raw_label": "(C)",
        "text": "Because it is covered under the inclusive definition of \"transfer\" as an\nextinguishment of any rights in the capital asset."
      },
      {
        "label": "D",
        "raw_label": "(D)",
        "text": "Because the face value of the shares remains unchanged, constituting a deemed\ntransfer."
      }
    ]
  },

  "before": {
    "stem": "68. The Supreme Court clarified a principle regarding the computation of capital gains/loss\nunder Section 48 of the Income Tax Act. What was this clarification?",
    "options": [
      {
        "label": "A",
        "raw_label": "(A)",
        "text": "That the reduction of share capital must result in a change in the percentage of\nshareholding."
      },
      {
        "label": "B",
        "raw_label": "(B)",
        "text": "That the face value of the shares must be reduced for the transfer to be valid."
      },
      {
        "label": "C",
        "raw_label": "(C)",
        "text": "That the transfer must be a sale or relinquishment, and not merely an\nextinguishment of rights."
      },
      {
        "label": "D",
        "raw_label": "(D)",
        "text": "That receipt of some consideration in lieu of the extinguishment of rights is not a\ncondition precedent for the computation of capital gains/loss."
      }
    ]

  "rule": "literal_source_boundaries_and_primary_options",
  "before": {
    "stem": "74. Which of the following is/are CORRECT proposition(s) as regards the law on damages for\nthe breach of contract under section 74 of the Indian Contract Act:",
    "options": [
      {
        "label": "A",
        "raw_label": "(A)",
        "text": "Where a sum is named in the contract as a liquidated amount payable by way of\ndamages, only reasonable compensation can be awarded not exceeding the amount\nso stated."
      },
      {
        "label": "B",
        "raw_label": "(B)",
        "text": "In cases where the amount fixed is in the nature of penalty, only reasonable\ncompensation can be awarded, not exceeding the penalty so stated."
      },
      {
        "label": "C",
        "raw_label": "(C)",
        "text": "The expression ‘whether or not actual damage or loss is proved to have been caused\nthereby’ in section 74 means that in every case the proof of actual damage or loss\nhas been dispensed with."
      },
      {
        "label": "D",
        "raw_label": "(D)",
        "text": "Both (A) and (B)."
      }
    ]
  },

d3905f6d3c31af4cdf5d47d3e6380179c5fd2c8f55e489648d140783b06a0d3b:p0032:l0013:question
{
  "question_id": "d3905f6d3c31af4cdf5d47d3e6380179c5fd2c8f55e489648d140783b06a0d3b:p0032:l0013:question",
  "rule": "literal_source_boundaries_and_primary_options",
  "before": {
    "options": [
      {
        "label": "A",
        "raw_label": "(A)",
        "text": "It is, in general, open to the contracting parties to confer by their agreement\njurisdiction on a court which does not possess the jurisdiction under the law."
      },
      {
        "label": "B",
        "raw_label": "(B)",
        "text": "It is not open to the contracting parties to confer by their agreement jurisdiction on\na court which does not possess the jurisdiction under the law."
      },
      {
        "label": "C",
        "raw_label": "(C)",
        "text": "It is open to the contracting parties to confer by their written and registered\nagreement jurisdiction on a court which does not possess the jurisdiction under the\nlaw."
      },
      {
        "label": "D",
        "raw_label": "(D)",
        "text": "If it is absolutely in the interest of the contracting parties, then only it is open to\nthe contracting parties to confer by their agreement jurisdiction on a court which\ndoes not possess the jurisdiction under the law."
      }
    ]

    "options": [
      {
        "label": "A",
        "raw_label": "(A)",
        "text": "Jurisdiction of civil courts is created by statute and cannot be created or conferred\nby consent of the parties upon a court which has not been granted jurisdiction by\nthe law."
      },
      {
        "label": "B",
        "raw_label": "(B)",
        "text": "Where two or more courts have under the law jurisdiction to try a suit or\nproceeding, an agreement between the parties that the dispute between them will\nbe tried in one of such courts, is not contrary to public policy."
      },
      {
        "label": "C",
        "raw_label": "(C)",
        "text": "Ouster clauses can oust the jurisdiction only of civil courts and not of the High\nCourt, provided such jurisdiction exists in the High Court on account of part of\ncause of action having arisen with its territorial jurisdiction."
      },
      {
        "label": "D",
        "raw_label": "(D)",
        "text": "An ouster clause is valid even if it confers exclusive jurisdiction on a court that\notherwise has no territorial or pecuniary jurisdiction over the matter."
      }
    ]

d3905f6d3c31af4cdf5d47d3e6380179c5fd2c8f55e489648d140783b06a0d3b:p0033:l0000:question
{
  "question_id": "d3905f6d3c31af4cdf5d47d3e6380179c5fd2c8f55e489648d140783b06a0d3b:p0033:l0000:question",
  "rule": "literal_source_boundaries_and_primary_options",
  "before": {
    "stem": "78. Which of the following cannot be a condition for an exclusive jurisdiction clause in a\ncontract to be valid:",
    "options": [
      {
        "label": "A",
        "raw_label": "(A)",
        "text": "It should be in consonance with section 28 of the Indian Contract Act, i.e. it should\nnot absolutely restrict any party from initiating legal proceedings pertaining to the\ncontract."
      },
      {
        "label": "B",
        "raw_label": "(B)",
        "text": "The court which the parties have chosen for exclusive jurisdiction must be\ncompetent to have such jurisdiction."
      },
      {
        "label": "C",
        "raw_label": "(C)",
        "text": "The parties must either impliedly or explicitly agree to subject themselves to the\njurisdiction of a specific court for the resolution of their contractual dispute."
      },
      {
        "label": "D",
        "raw_label": "(D)",
        "text": "The parties agree to the jurisdiction of a court that does not have the jurisdiction\nover the matter under the general law."
      }
    ]
  },

  "rule": "literal_source_boundaries_and_primary_options",
  "before": {
    "stem": "84. Which of the following propositions is/are CORRECT about the award of damages in\ncases where there is violation of fundamental rights:",
    "options": [
      {
        "label": "A",
        "raw_label": "(A)",
        "text": "Constitutional courts can in appropriate cases of serious violation of life and liberty\nof the individuals award punitive damages."
      },
      {
        "label": "B",
        "raw_label": "(B)",
        "text": "Owing to lack of legislation, the Courts dealing with the cases of tortious claims\nagainst State and its officials are not following a uniform pattern while deciding\nthose claims and this, at times, leads to undesirable consequences and arbitrary\nfixation of compensation amount."
      },
      {
        "label": "C",
        "raw_label": "(C)",
        "text": "Both (A) and (B)."
      },
      {
        "label": "D",
        "raw_label": "(D)",
        "text": "Neither (A) nor (B)."
      }
    ]
  },

d3905f6d3c31af4cdf5d47d3e6380179c5fd2c8f55e489648d140783b06a0d3b:p0045:l0000:question
{
  "question_id": "d3905f6d3c31af4cdf5d47d3e6380179c5fd2c8f55e489648d140783b06a0d3b:p0045:l0000:question",
  "rule": "literal_source_boundaries_and_primary_options",
  "before": {
    "stem": "114. In which of the following landmark judgements, the Supreme Court held that when an\nassociation or society of apartment owners employs workers for personal services to its\nmembers, those workers do not qualify as workmen under the Act and the association is\nnot an “Industry” under the Industrial Disputes Act?",
    "options": [
      {
        "label": "A",
        "raw_label": "(A)",
        "text": "Som Vihar Apartment Owners’ Housing Maintenance Society Ltd v. Workmen,\n2009 SC"
      },
      {
        "label": "B",
        "raw_label": "(B)",
        "text": "Anand Vihar Apartment Owners’ Society Ltd. V. Workmen, 2024 SC"
      },
      {
        "label": "C",
        "raw_label": "(C)",
        "text": "Kanchanjunga Building Employees Union v. Kanchanjunga Flat Owner’s Society\n&Anr., 2024 SC"

  "before": {
    "stem": "24. What is the phrase “Presumptions are like bats, flitting in the twilight but disappearing\nin the sunshine of facts” indicate?",
    "options": [
      {
        "label": "A",
        "raw_label": "(A)",
        "text": "Presumption shifts the burden of proof to the party against whom the presumption\noperates, but the burden shifts back to the original party once rebutting facts are\npresented"
      },
      {
        "label": "B",
        "raw_label": "(B)",
        "text": "Presumption is a substantive piece of evidence and it completely relieve the\nprosecution of its burden of proof, as longs as the presumption is established in\nthe beginning of the trial"
      },
      {
        "label": "C",
        "raw_label": "(C)",
        "text": "There are different categories of presumptions and the highest degree of\npresumption shifts the burden of proof permanently to the accused, who must\ndisprove the presumption beyond reasonable doubt"
      },
      {
        "label": "D",
        "raw_label": "(D)",
        "text": "Presumptions are irrefutable facts that, once established, cannot be negated by\nevidence brought forth in the case"
      }
    ]
  },

  "rule": "literal_source_boundaries_and_primary_options",
  "before": {
    "stem": "53. Which of the following needs to be considered while entertaining an application for\nremission under the provisions of Cr.P.C., 1973?",
    "options": [
      {
        "label": "A",
        "raw_label": "(A)",
        "text": "The application for remission under Section 432 of the Cr.P.C., 1973 could be\nonly before the Government of the State within whose territorial jurisdiction\nthe applicant was convicted (appropriate Government) and not before any other\nGovernment within whose territorial jurisdiction the applicant may have been\ntransferred on conviction or where the offence has occurred"
      },
      {
        "label": "B",
        "raw_label": "(B)",
        "text": "A consideration for remission must be by way of an application under Section 432 of\nthe Cr.P.C., 1973 which has to be made by the convict or on his behalf. In the first\ninstance whether there is compliance with Section 433A of the Cr.P.C., 1973 must\nbe noted in as much as a person serving a life sentence cannot seek remission\nunless fourteen years of imprisonment has been completed"
      },

        "label": "C",
        "raw_label": "(C)",
        "text": "Both (A) and (B)"
      },

        "label": "D",
        "raw_label": "(D)",
        "text": "Only (A)"
      }
    ]

  "rule": "literal_source_boundaries_and_primary_options",
  "before": {
    "stem": "56. Which of the following is the effect of non-registration of a compulsorily registrable\ndocument?",
    "options": [
      {
        "label": "A",
        "raw_label": "(A)",
        "text": "The unregistered document cannot be adduced in evidence of any transaction\naffecting such property"
      },
      {
        "label": "B",
        "raw_label": "(B)",
        "text": "As long as the terms, grant or disposition is in writing and fulfils the criteria of\nS. 91 of the Indian Evidence Act, it will be admitted as evidence"
      },
      {
        "label": "C",
        "raw_label": "(C)",
        "text": "Procedure is a handmaid of justice and registration is merely a procedural\nrequirement. Non registration does not make the document less admissible in\ncourt"
      },
      {
        "label": "D",
        "raw_label": "(D)",
        "text": "The unregistered document can be adduced in evidence if the party adducing it\nis able to prove its bonafide"
      }
    ]
  },

    "stem": "94.   "question_id": "d3905f6d3c31af4cdf5d47d3e6380179c5fd2c8f55e489648d140783b06a0d3b:p0084:l0001:question",
  "rule": "literal_source_boundaries_and_primary_options",
  "before": {
    "stem": "98. The trinity of Articles 14, 15, and 16 has provided a tool to march towards social and\neconomic equality. Emphasis has been given to affirmative action so as to give a special\ntreatment to the underprivileged so that they can march forward. Reservations in the\nmatters of education and in public employment have been used to provide a special\ntreatment to the backward classes. What are the other articles of the Constitution\nalong with, the objective of the Constitution to achieve social economic equality may\nbe achieved?"
  },

d3905f6d3c31af4cdf5d47d3e6380179c5fd2c8f55e489648d140783b06a0d3b:p0084:l0012:question
{
  "question_id": "d3905f6d3c31af4cdf5d47d3e6380179c5fd2c8f55e489648d140783b06a0d3b:p0084:l0012:question",
  "rule": "literal_source_boundaries_and_primary_options",
  "before": {
    "stem": "99. Hon’ble Justice B.R. Gavai, in the above-mentioned judgment held that, “sub-classification\namongst the Scheduled Castes for giving more beneficial treatment is permissible in\nlaw”. He also gave some criteria on which the sub-classification may be implemented\nby the State. Which of the following is that criteria?",
    "options": [
      {
        "label": "A",
        "raw_label": "(A)",
        "text": "The criteria for exclusion of the creamy layer from the Scheduled Castes and\nScheduled Tribes for the purpose of affirmative action could be different from the\ncriteria as applicable to the Other Backward Classes"
      },
      {
        "label": "B",
        "raw_label": "(B)",
        "text": "Sub-classification would be permissible only if there is a reservation for a\nsub-class as well as the larger class"
      },
      {
        "label": "C",
        "raw_label": "(C)",
        "text": "That while doing so, the State will have to justify the same on the basis of empirical\ndata that a sub-class in whose favour such more beneficial treatment is provided\nis not adequately represented"
      },
      {
        "label": "D",
        "raw_label": "(D)",
        "text": "All of the above"
      }
    ]
  },
  "after": {
    "stem": "99. Hon’ble Justice B.R. Gavai, in the above-mentioned judgment held that, “sub-classification amongst the Scheduled Castes for giving more beneficial treatment is permissible in law”. He also gave some criteria on which the sub-classification may be implemented by the State. Which of the following is that criteria?",
    "options": [
      {
        "label": "A",
        "raw_label": "(A)",
        "text": "The criteria for exclusion of the creamy layer from the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes for the purpose of affirmative action could be different from the criteria as applicable to the Other Backward Classes"
      },
      {
        "label": "B",
        "raw_label": "(B)",
        "text": "Sub-classification would be permissible only if there is a reservation for a sub-class as well as the larger class"
      },
      {
        "label": "C",
        "raw_label": "(C)",
        "text": "That while doing so, the State will have to justify the same on the basis of empirical data that a sub-class in whose favour such more beneficial treatment is provided is not adequately represented"
      },
      {
        "label": "D",
        "raw_label": "(D)",
        "text": "All of the above"
      }
    ]
  },

d3905f6d3c31af4cdf5d47d3e6380179c5fd2c8f55e489648d140783b06a0d3b:p0088:l0001:question
{
  "question_id": "d3905f6d3c31af4cdf5d47d3e6380179c5fd2c8f55e489648d140783b06a0d3b:p0088:l0001:question",
  "rule": "literal_source_boundaries_and_primary_options",
  "before": {
    "stem": "109. Articles 323-A and 323-B of the Indian Constitution for the establishment of tribunal\nto adjudicate disputes in specific matters. While both articles deal with tribunals, there\nare key differences in their scope and application. Which of the following statement\ncorrectly reflects the distinction between Articles 323-A and 323-B?",
    "options": [
      {
        "label": "A",
        "raw_label": "(A)",
        "text": "Article 323-A exclusively deals with administrative tribunals for public service\nmatters, while Article 323-B deals with the tribunals for a wider range of subjects\nincluding taxation and land reforms"
      },
      {
        "label": "B",
        "raw_label": "(B)",
        "text": "While tribunals under Article 323-A can be established only by Parliament,\ntribunals under Article 323-B can only be established by State legislature, with\nmatters falling within their legislative competence"
      },
      {
        "label": "C",
        "raw_label": "(C)",
        "text": "Under Article 323-A, only one tribunal for centre and no tribunal for state may\nbe established. As far as Article 323-B is concerned, there is no hierarchy of\ntribunals"
      },
      {
        "label": "D",
        "raw_label": "(D)",
        "text": "Article 323-A grant tribunals the power to hear appeals directly from the Supreme\nCourt, by passing the High Court. Under Article 323-B there is no such power"
      }
    ]
  },
  "after": {

    "stem": "14. the Supreme Court has recognised in several decisions that in cases requiring urgent\nadministrative action or in exigencies, it may not always be possible to give full effect to\nthe principles of natural justice without rendering the administrative action redundant in the\ncircumstances.     "options": [
      {
        "label": "A",
        "raw_label": "(a)",
        "text": "the administrator may choose to not follow principles of natural justice in case of\nemergency scenarios, where time does not permit such compliance, without recording\ntheir reasons in writing."

        "label": "B",
        "raw_label": "(B)",
        "text": "the administrator may choose to not follow principles of natural justice in case of\nemergency scenarios, where time does not permit such compliance, but must record\ntheir reasons in writing."

      {
        "label": "C",
        "raw_label": "(C)",
        "text": "the administrator may provide for a post-decisional remedial hearing wherever pre-\ndecisional hearing is not possible."
      },

        "label": "D",
        "raw_label": "(d)",
        "text": "none of the above."
      }
    ]
  },

    "stem": "18. Which of the following statements reflect the correct position of law for promissory estoppel\nagainst Governments?",

        "label": "A",
        "raw_label": "(a)",

d3905f6d3c31af4cdf5d47d3e6380179c5fd2c8f55e489648d140783b06a0d3b:p0105:l0001:question
{
  "question_id": "d3905f6d3c31af4cdf5d47d3e6380179c5fd2c8f55e489648d140783b06a0d3b:p0105:l0001:question",
  "rule": "literal_source_boundaries_and_primary_options",
  "before": {
    "options": [
      {
        "label": "A",
        "raw_label": "(a)",
        "text": "the doctrine of promissory estoppel stands diluted where the Government claims that\nit is in the public interest to go back on its promise or actions."
      },
      {
        "label": "B",
        "raw_label": "(B)",
        "text": "the doctrine of promissory estoppel overrides any purported claims of public interest\nby the Government."
      },
      {
        "label": "C",
        "raw_label": "(C)",
        "text": "Permitting a public interest exception is against the interests of justice, equity and good\nconscience as it is a self-serving claim for the Government."
      },
      {
        "label": "D",
        "raw_label": "(d)",
        "text": "Both (B) and (C)."
      }
    ]
  },

{
  "question_id": "d3905f6d3c31af4cdf5d47d3e6380179c5fd2c8f55e489648d140783b06a0d3b:p0106:l0016:question",
  "rule": "literal_source_boundaries_and_primary_options",
  "before": {
    "stem": "21. Hypothetically, if the Gambian state was to exercise criminal jurisdiction over the persons\nresponsible for Crimes of Genocide, then such jurisdiction would be called as:",
    "options": [
      {
        "label": "A",
        "raw_label": "(a)",
        "text": "extra-territorial jurisdiction"

        "raw_label": "(d)",
        "text": "States are bound by Peremptory norms of general international law (Jus Cogens) only\nwhen they have given express consent to it in writing."

{

  "rule": "literal_source_boundaries_and_primary_options",
  "before": {
    "stem": "30. Which of the following statements is not true with respect to ‘customary international\nlaw’?",
    "options": [
      {
        "label": "A",
        "raw_label": "(a)",
        "text": "in the asylum case 1950, iCJ declared that a customary rule must be ‘in accordance\nwith a constant and uniform usage practiced by the States in question’."
      },
      {
        "label": "B",
        "raw_label": "(B)",
        "text": "in the north Sea Continental Shelf cases, 1969, iCJ remarked that state practice had\nto be ‘both extensive and virtually uniform in the sense of the provision invoked’."
      },
      {
        "label": "C",
        "raw_label": "(C)",
        "text": "in the nicaragua v. United States case, 1986, iCJ said that it was not necessary that\nthe practice in question had to be ‘in absolutely rigorous conformity’ with the purported\ncustomary rule."
      },
      {
        "label": "D",
        "raw_label": "(d)",
        "text": "in the Right of Passage over indian territory case, 1960, iCJ denied the existence of\nlocal custom between the two states."
      }
    ]
  },

d3905f6d3c31af4cdf5d47d3e6380179c5fd2c8f55e489648d140783b06a0d3b:p0113:l0022:question
{
  "question_id": "d3905f6d3c31af4cdf5d47d3e6380179c5fd2c8f55e489648d140783b06a0d3b:p0113:l0022:question",
  "rule": "literal_source_boundaries_and_primary_options",
  "before": {
    "stem": "45. The Tenth Schedule specifies five defense that a member may take recourse to shield\nthemselves from the consequences of the anti-defection law. Which among the following\nis not a defense?",
    "options": [
      {
        "label": "A",
        "raw_label": "(a)",
        "text": "in cases where the original political party of a member is found to have merged with\nanother political party under Paragraph 4(1)(a), members of the original political party\nare protected from being disqualified if they have not accepted such merger and have\nopted to function as a separate group."
      },
      {
        "label": "B",
        "raw_label": "(B)",
        "text": "Members who have been elected to the office of the Speaker or the Deputy Speaker\n(or the Chairman or the deputy Chairman as the case may be) in Parliament or in the\nLegislative Assemblies of States are exempted from disqualification under the Tenth\nSchedule if they voluntarily give up the membership of their political party by reason of\ntheir election to such office and do not re-join the political party or become a member\nof another political party so long as they continue to hold such office. Further, they are\nnot disqualified if they re-join the political party which they gave up membership of, after\nceasing to hold office."
      },
      {
        "label": "C",
        "raw_label": "(C)",
        "text": "Disqualification on ground of defection not to apply in case of split. Where a member of\na House makes a claim that he and any other members of his legislature party constitute\nthe group representing a faction, which has arisen as a result of a split in his original\npolitical party and such group consists of not less than one-third of the members of such\nlegislature party."
      },
      {
        "label": "D",
        "raw_label": "(D)",
        "text": "A member is protected from being disqualified if the political party to which they belong\nhas condoned their actions in voting or abstaining from voting contrary to the directions\nissued by such political party, within fifteen days from such voting or abstention."
      }
    ]
  },

        "text": "a force majeure clause ensures that non-performance is no breach because no\nperformance was due in the circumstances which have occurred."

  "before": {
    "options": [
      {
        "label": "A",
        "raw_label": "(a)",
        "text": "the courts have the general power to absolve a party from the performance of its part\nof the contract if its performance has become onerous on account of an unforeseen\nturn of events.\n\n"
      },
      {
        "label": "B",
        "raw_label": "(B)",
        "text": "if a contract contains a term according to which it would stand discharged on the\nhappening of certain contingencies, dissolution of the contract would take place under\nthe terms of the contract itself and such cases would be outside the purview of section\n56 of the indian Contract act; such cases have to be dealt with under section 32 of the\nindian Contract act."
      },
      {
        "label": "C",
        "raw_label": "(C)",
        "text": "the application of the doctrine of frustration must always be within narrow limits."
      },

d3905f6d3c31af4cdf5d47d3e6380179c5fd2c8f55e489648d140783b06a0d3b:p0130:l0015:question

  "question_id": "d3905f6d3c31af4cdf5d47d3e6380179c5fd2c8f55e489648d140783b06a0d3b:p0130:l0015:question",
  "rule": "literal_source_boundaries_and_primary_options",
  "before": {
    "stem": "99. in Energy Watchdog v. Central Electricity Regulatory Commission, the Supreme Court\nfound that the fundamental basis of the power purchase agreements (PPas) between the\nparties was not premised on the price of coal imported from indonesia. in fact, in the PPas,\nthere was a clause providing that changes in the cost of fuel, or the agreement becoming\nonerous to perform, are not treated as force majeure. therefore, on the ground of the rise\nin price of indonesian coal, the Court held that:",
    "options": [
      {
        "label": "A",
        "raw_label": "(a)",
        "text": "alternative modes of performance were available, albeit at a higher price; and that alone\ncould not lead to the contract, as a whole, being frustrated."
      },
      {
        "label": "B",
        "raw_label": "(B)",
        "text": "the contract was frustrated on account of an unexpected rise in the price of indonesian\ncoal excusing the generating company from performing its part of the contract."
      },
      {
        "label": "C",
        "raw_label": "(C)",
        "text": "even though the PPas are not frustrated, on account of an unexpected rise in the price\nof indonesian coal, the force majeure clause could be invoked in the given case to\nextend relief to the generating company."
      },
      {
        "label": "D",
        "raw_label": "(d)",
        "text": "the contract was frustrated on account of an unexpected rise in the price of indonesian\ncoal because the performance of an act might not be literally impossible, but it may\nbe impracticable and useless from the point of view of the object and purpose of the\ncontract."
      }
    ]
  },

{
  "question_id": "d3905f6d3c31af4cdf5d47d3e6380179c5fd2c8f55e489648d140783b06a0d3b:p0131:l0021:question",
  "rule": "literal_source_boundaries_and_primary_options",
  "before": {
    "stem": "101. At present, which of the following is the correct proposition as regards the specific performance\nof a contract:",
    "options": [
      {
        "label": "A",
        "raw_label": "(A)",
        "text": "As a general rule, the specific performance of a contract is now a general remedy."
      },
      {
        "label": "B",
        "raw_label": "(B)",
        "text": "As a general rule, the specific performance of a contract is enforced by the court when\nthere exists no standard for ascertaining actual damage caused by the non-performance\nof the act agreed to be done."
      },
      {
        "label": "C",
        "raw_label": "(C)",
        "text": "As a general rule, the specific performance of a contract is enforced by the court when\nthe act agreed to be done is such that compensation in money for its non-performance\nwould not afford adequate relief."
      },
      {
        "label": "D",
        "raw_label": "(d)",
        "text": "Both (B) and (C)."
      }
    ]
  },

        "label": "A",
        "raw_label": "(a)",
        "text": "Yes, every statement made by a Minister, inconsistent with the rights of a citizen under Part-iii of the Constitution, will constitute a violation of the constitutional rights and becomes actionable as a constitutional tort."
      },
      {

        "raw_label": "(B)",
        "text": "Yes, if as a consequence of such a statement, any act of omission or commission is done by the officers resulting in harm or loss to a person/citizen, then the same may be actionable as a constitutional tort."
      },
      {

        "raw_label": "(C)",
        "text": "no, in no case a statement by a Minister is actionable as a constitutional tort."

      },
      {
        "label": "B",
        "raw_label": "(B)",
        "text": "the jurisprudential concept of negligence is the same in civil and criminal laws, and\nwhat may be negligence in civil law is necessarily a negligence in criminal law."
      },
      {
        "label": "C",
        "raw_label": "(C)",
        "text": "a professional may be held liable for negligence, and the standard to be applied for\njudging, whether the person charged has been negligent or not, would be that of an\nordinary competent person exercising ordinary skill in that profession."
      },
      {
        "label": "D",
        "raw_label": "(d)",
        "text": "it is not possible for every professional to possess the highest level of expertise or\nskills in that branch which he practices; a highly skilled professional may be possessed\nof better qualities, but that cannot be made the basis or the yardstick for judging the\nperformance of the professional proceeded against on indictment of negligence."
      }

  "before": {
    "stem": "118. Which of the following propositions is correct as regards the liability of medical\npractitioners:",
    "options": [
      {
        "label": "A",
        "raw_label": "(a)",
        "text": "Medical practitioners are immune from a claim for damages on the ground of negligence,\nas they belong to the medical profession."
      },
      {
        "label": "B",
        "raw_label": "(B)",
        "text": "Medical practitioners are immune from a claim for damages on the ground of negligence,\nas they are governed by the national Medical Commission act, 2019."
      },
      {
        "label": "C",
        "raw_label": "(C)",
        "text": "Medical practitioners are immune from a claim for damages on the ground of negligence,\nas the ethics and Medical Registration Board has the power to regulate professional\nconduct and promote medical ethics."
      },
      {
        "label": "D",
        "raw_label": "(d)",
        "text": "Medical practitioners, though belonging to the medical profession, are not immune from\na claim for damages on the ground of negligence."
      }
    ]

d3905f6d3c31af4cdf5d47d3e6380179c5fd2c8f55e489648d140783b06a0d3b:p0137:l0017:question
{
  "question_id": "d3905f6d3c31af4cdf5d47d3e6380179c5fd2c8f55e489648d140783b06a0d3b:p0137:l0017:question",
  "rule": "literal_source_boundaries_and_primary_options",
  "before": {
    "stem": "120. now, a large number of private hospitals, nursing homes and clinics have emerged. in view\nof the good reputation they have built, patients go there for treatment in large numbers.\nthese hospitals provide the medical treatment to those patients through doctors employed\nby them or by doctors who work there on some arrangement. these hospitals raise the bills\nfor the fees and medical treatment provided to those patients by all such doctors. in such\ncircumstances, if the patient suffers injury due to negligence of the doctors, then:",
    "options": [
      {
        "label": "A",
        "raw_label": "(a)",
        "text": "the hospitals would be equally liable for damages, on the principles of vicarious liability\nor on the principles analogous to vicarious liability, and these hospitals cannot shove\noff their responsibility and liability to pay compensation for the damages suffered by the\npatients due to the negligence of the doctors provided by these very hospitals."
      },
      {
        "label": "B",
        "raw_label": "(B)",
        "text": "the hospitals would not at all be held liable for damages."
      },
      {
        "label": "C",
        "raw_label": "(C)",
        "text": "the hospitals would not at all be held liable for damages; but the doctors could not\nshove off their liability for negligence."
      },
      {
        "label": "D",
        "raw_label": "(d)",
        "text": "neither the hospitals nor the doctors are held liable, as no one can guarantee the desired\nresult in the medical profession."
      }
    ]
  },
  "after": {
    "stem": "120. now, a large number of private hospitals, nursing homes and clinics have emerged. in view of the good reputation they have built, patients go there for treatment in large numbers. these hospitals provide the medical treatment to those patients through doctors employed by them or by doctors who work there on some arrangement. these hospitals raise the bills for the fees and medical treatment provided to those patients by all such doctors. in such circumstances, if the patient suffers injury due to negligence of the doctors, then:",
    "options": [
      {
        "label": "A",
        "raw_label": "(a)",
        "text": "the hospitals would be equally liable for damages, on the principles of vicarious liability or on the principles analogous to vicarious liability, and these hospitals cannot shove off their responsibility and liability to pay compensation for the damages suffered by the patients due to the negligence of the doctors provided by these very hospitals."
      },

{

      {
        "label": "A",
        "raw_label": "(A)",
        "text": "An Ordinance which is not laid before the Legislature in the manner\nprescribed by Article 213 shall not have any legal effect and consequences."
      },

        "label": "B",
        "raw_label": "(b)",
        "text": "An Ordinance which is not laid before the Legislature in the manner prescribed\nby Article 213 shall be void from the date that it should have obtained\napproval."
      },

        "label": "C",
        "raw_label": "(C)",
        "text": "An Ordinance which is not laid before the Legislature in the manner prescribed\nby Article 213 shall be void from the date the ordinance is replaced by a law\nmade by the Legislature to replace the Ordinance."
      },
      {
        "label": "D",
        "raw_label": "(d)",
        "text": "An Ordinance which is not laid before the Legislature in the manner prescribed\nby Article 213 shall be considered as a temporary statute."

d3905f6d3c31af4cdf5d47d3e6380179c5fd2c8f55e489648d140783b06a0d3b:p0152:l0011:question
{
  "question_id": "d3905f6d3c31af4cdf5d47d3e6380179c5fd2c8f55e489648d140783b06a0d3b:p0152:l0011:question",
  "rule": "literal_source_boundaries_and_primary_options",
  "before": {
    "stem": "19. Section 6 of the General Clauses Act, 1897 protects rights, privileges, obligations\nand liabilities in cases of repeal of an enactment. the majority in KK Singh held\nthat:\ni. the Ordinance that ‘ceases to operate’ is distinct from a law that is void.\nii. An Ordinance that ‘ceases to operate’ is distinct from a temporary statute.\niii. An Ordinance that ‘ceases to operate’ is distinct from a repealed statute.\niv. An Ordinance that ‘ceases to operate’ is not ‘saved’ in the absence of any\n‘savings clause’ in Article 213."
  },
  "after": {

        "text": "that a cryptic phone call, without complete details and information about the\ncommission of a cognizable offence cannot always be treated as a F.i.r."
      },
      {
        "label": "B",
        "raw_label": "(b)",
        "text": "that non-reading-over of the recorded complaint by the police to the informant\nwill vitiate the recording of the F.i.r."
      },
      {
        "label": "C",
        "raw_label": "(C)",
        "text": "that F.i.r.s are substantive pieces of evidence at the trial and can be duly\nproved to establish the facts in issue at a trial."

        "label": "D",
        "raw_label": "(d)",
        "text": "that F.i.r.s are necessarily hearsay statements and cannot be relied upon to\nprove the truth of the matters asserted therein."
      }
    ]

d3905f6d3c31af4cdf5d47d3e6380179c5fd2c8f55e489648d140783b06a0d3b:p0160:l0001:question
{
  "question_id": "d3905f6d3c31af4cdf5d47d3e6380179c5fd2c8f55e489648d140783b06a0d3b:p0160:l0001:question",
  "rule": "literal_source_boundaries_and_primary_options",
  "before": {
    "stem": "43. upon receipt of a complaint disclosing the commission of a cognizable offence from\nan informant, the station house officer of a police station proceeds to record the\nsubstance of the complaint in the Station House diary. thereafter, he proceeds\nto conduct investigation by going to the spot of the incident, collecting materials\nfrom the scene, and recording statements of persons he believes have information\nabout the alleged crime. On the next day, he calls the informant to the police station\nagain, and this time, proceeds to record a formal F.i.r. for the offences. He then\ngives a copy of the registered F.i.r. to the informant and sends him home. the\nduly registered F.i.r. can be challenged on which of the following grounds?",
    "options": [
      {
        "label": "A",
        "raw_label": "(A)",
        "text": "that the police officer has not followed the mandatory procedure of sending a\ncopy of the F.i.r. to the jurisdictional magistrate upon registration."
      },
      {
        "label": "B",
        "raw_label": "(b)",
        "text": "that the statement recorded as the F.i.r. is a hearsay statement made by the\npolice officer himself and therefore cannot be admissible in evidence."
      },
      {
        "label": "C",
        "raw_label": "(C)",
        "text": "that the recorded F.i.r. becomes a statement under Section 161, Code of\nCriminal Procedure, 1973, because the Station House diary entry will be\nconsidered the F.i.r."
      },
      {
        "label": "D",
        "raw_label": "(d)",
        "text": "that the procedure set out in Section 190, Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973\nhas been violated by the police officer."
      }
    ]
  },
  "after": {

  "before": {
    "stem": "44. in the case of Aghnoo Nagesia v. State of Bihar, Air 1966 SC 119, the accused\nhimself walked to the police station and registered an F.i.r. against himself for the\nmurder of his family members. there was no formal information of the commission\nof the offence prior to the accused himself having the F.i.r. registered. Per the\njudgment in the case, such an F.i.r. would be considered:",
    "options": [
      {
        "label": "A",
        "raw_label": "(A)",
        "text": "Violative of right against self-incrimination under Article 20(3) of the\nConstitution of India."
      },
      {
        "label": "B",
        "raw_label": "(b)",
        "text": "A statement that cannot be proved as a confession hit by Section 25, Indian\nEvidence Act, 1872."
      },
      {
        "label": "C",
        "raw_label": "(C)",
        "text": "A statement that can be used as substantive evidence against its maker, since\nthere was no accusation against him at the time he made the statement."
      },
      {
        "label": "D",
        "raw_label": "(d)",
        "text": "A statement that can be retracted by the accused person at the time of trial,\nand thereafter the commission of the offence cannot be proved."
      }
    ]
  },

d3905f6d3c31af4cdf5d47d3e6380179c5fd2c8f55e489648d140783b06a0d3b:p0161:l0018:question
{
  "question_id": "d3905f6d3c31af4cdf5d47d3e6380179c5fd2c8f55e489648d140783b06a0d3b:p0161:l0018:question",
  "rule": "literal_source_boundaries_and_primary_options",
  "before": {
    "stem": "48. An F.i.r. is considered the first information of the commission of a cognizable\noffence. Where the information discloses the commission of both cognizable offences\nas well as non-cognizable offences as part of the same facts, such information must\nbe treated in the following manner:",
    "options": [
      {
        "label": "A",
        "raw_label": "(A)",
        "text": "the entire information will be treated as disclosing cognizable offences and\nregistered as an F.i.r."
      },
      {
        "label": "B",
        "raw_label": "(b)",
        "text": "the police officer will sever the parts disclosing non-cognizable offences and\nshall only register the parts disclosing cognizable offences."
      },
      {
        "label": "C",
        "raw_label": "(C)",
        "text": "the police officer shall refer the informant to the jurisdictional magistrate for\na direction to register the F.i.r., and thereafter, once such direction is received,\nregister the F.i.r."
      },
      {
        "label": "D",
        "raw_label": "(d)",
        "text": "the F.i.r. registered, which contains information of non-cognizable offences,\nis subject to confirmation by a magistrate under Sections 156 and 157\nof Cr.P.C."
      }
    ]
  },
  "after": {
    "stem": "48. An F.i.r. is considered the first information of the commission of a cognizable offence. Where the information discloses the commission of both cognizable offences as well as non-cognizable offences as part of the same facts, such information must be treated in the following manner:",
    "options": [
      {
        "label": "A",

        "text": "the entire information will be treated as disclosing cognizable offences and registered as an F.i.r."
      },
      {
        "label": "B",
        "raw_label": "(b)",
        "text": "the police officer will sever the parts disclosing non-cognizable offences and shall only register the parts disclosing cognizable offences."
      },
      {
        "label": "C",
        "raw_label": "(C)",
        "text": "the police officer shall refer the informant to the jurisdictional magistrate for a direction to register the F.i.r., and thereafter, once such direction is received, register the F.i.r."
      },
      {
        "label": "D",
        "raw_label": "(d)",
        "text": "the F.i.r. registered, which contains information of non-cognizable offences, is subject to confirmation by a magistrate under Sections 156 and 157 of Cr.P.C."

    "stem": "49. the power of the police to launch an investigation is provided for under Sections\n154 and 157 of Cr.P.",

        "text": "the threshold to be met for launching an investigation\nunder Section 157, according to Lalita Kumari, is"

        "text": "Higher than the requirement under Section 154 of Cr.P."

  "before": {
    "stem": "50. According to the decision of the Supreme Court in Lalita Kumari, the police may not\nconsider the genuineness of information disclosing the commission of a cognisable\noffence at the time of registering an F.i.r. What does this mean?",
    "options": [
      {
        "label": "A",
        "raw_label": "(A)",
        "text": "that the informant must be believed for the purposes of registering the\nF.i.r."

        "raw_label": "(b)",
        "text": "that the information must be taken as true for the purposes of registering the\nF.i.r."
      },
      {
        "label": "C",
        "raw_label": "(C)",
        "text": "that the police cannot reject any information disclosing the commission of a\ncognisable offence on the basis of it being false."
      },
      {
        "label": "D",
        "raw_label": "(d)",
        "text": "All the above"
      }

    "stem": "55. Where primary evidence of an electronic record cannot be produced in court,\nand the secondary evidence is not accompanied by a certificate required under\nSection 65B(4), Indian Evidence Act, 1872, the court may:",
    "options": [
      {
        "label": "A",
        "raw_label": "(A)",
        "text": "Never admit such evidence"
      },
      {
        "label": "B",
        "raw_label": "(b)",
        "text": "may only admit such evidence where it is satisfied that procuring such a\ncertificate for the party adducing the document into evidence would result in\nunfair prejudice, and where the document is crucial evidence"
      },
      {
        "label": "C",
        "raw_label": "(C)",
        "text": "may admit such evidence if satisfied that the party adducing such evidence was\nunable to procure the certificate despite best efforts and that it was impossible\nfor them to do so"
      },
      {
        "label": "D",
        "raw_label": "(d)",
        "text": "Admit such evidence after a scrutiny of the fact it purports to prove, and only\ndo so for the proof of relevant facts, and never for the proof of facts in issue as\ndefined under Section 3, Indian Evidence Act, 1872.\nM 20\nPG"
      }
    ]
  },

d3905f6d3c31af4cdf5d47d3e6380179c5fd2c8f55e489648d140783b06a0d3b:p0165:l0001:question
{
  "question_id": "d3905f6d3c31af4cdf5d47d3e6380179c5fd2c8f55e489648d140783b06a0d3b:p0165:l0001:question",
  "rule": "literal_source_boundaries_and_primary_options",
  "before": {
    "stem": "56. A plaintiff seeks to adduce a secondary electronic record into evidence and does\nnot comply with the requirements under Section 65B, Indian Evidence Act, 1872,\nfor the same. the respondent does not object to the admission of such evidence\nat trial. Subsequently, upon appeal, a ground is taken by the original respondent\nthat such evidence should not have been admitted as it did not comply with the\nprocedure under Section 65B. relying on the Supreme Court’s judgment in Sonu\nv. State of Haryana, (2017) 8 SCC 570, the court should hold:",
    "options": [
      {
        "label": "A",
        "raw_label": "(A)",
        "text": "An appellate court should declare the evidence inadmissible in line with the\nmandatory nature of Section 65B."
      },
      {
        "label": "B",
        "raw_label": "(b)",
        "text": "An appellate court should remand the matter to trial declaring the said evidence\ninadmissible."
      },
      {
        "label": "C",
        "raw_label": "(C)",
        "text": "An objection to the method of proof cannot be raised at the appellate stage as\nthe original plaintiff cannot rectify the error."
      },
      {
        "label": "D",
        "raw_label": "(d)",
        "text": "Since the respondent did not object to the admissibility of the evidence, the\ndocument is held to be proved."
      }
    ]
  },
  "after": {

d3905f6d3c31af4cdf5d47d3e6380179c5fd2c8f55e489648d140783b06a0d3b:p0165:l0016:question
{
  "question_id": "d3905f6d3c31af4cdf5d47d3e6380179c5fd2c8f55e489648d140783b06a0d3b:p0165:l0016:question",
  "rule": "literal_source_boundaries_and_primary_options",
  "before": {
    "stem": "57. the Supreme Court in Anvar v. Basheer, (2014) 10 SCC 473, overruled the decision\nof State (NCT of Delhi) v. Navjot Sandhu, (2005) 11 SCC 600, on which of its\nholdings?",
    "options": [
      {
        "label": "A",
        "raw_label": "(A)",
        "text": "that in cases of criminal conspiracy, the method of proof of the conspiracy is\ncontrolled by Section 10, Indian Evidence Act, 1872, and not Section 65B."
      },
      {
        "label": "B",
        "raw_label": "(b)",
        "text": "that irrespective of compliance with Section 65B, contents of electronic\ndocuments could be proved through Sections 62-65 of the Indian Evidence\nAct, 1872."
      },
      {
        "label": "C",
        "raw_label": "(C)",
        "text": "that electronic documents being a special class of general documents, had to be\nproved through expert opinion under Section 45, Indian Evidence Act, 1872."
      },
      {
        "label": "D",
        "raw_label": "(d)",
        "text": "that the document sought to be proved must first be marked and then admitted\ninto evidence for its contents, and that this sequence may not be reversed."
      }
    ]
  },
  "after": {

  "question_id": "d3905f6d3c31af4cdf5d47d3e6380179c5fd2c8f55e489648d140783b06a0d3b:p0166:l0001:question",
  "rule": "literal_source_boundaries_and_primary_options",
  "before": {
    "printed_question_number": "5",
    "stem": "5 9. X gets his Will made. the final Will is drawn up by a scribe who takes down the\ndictation of the terms and averments of the document, and thereafter, the Will\nis executed by the testator. the execution of the Will is also attested to by two\nwitnesses. upon the death of X, the Will falls into controversy. Y, one of X’s sons,\nchallenges the validity of the Will. to prove due execution of the document, Z, X’s\nother son, who supports the Will, calls one of the attesting witnesses to court. this\nwitness states that he does not remember the due execution of the Will nor does he\nremember attesting the Will. thereafter, Z seeks to examine the scribe who wrote\nthe Will as a witness to its execution. Can the scribe be examined at this stage?",
    "options": [
      {
        "label": "A",
        "raw_label": "(A)",
        "text": "Yes, since one of the attesting witnesses has not recalled the execution, any\nother evidence is now admissible to prove execution under Section 71, Indian\nEvidence Act, 1872."
      },
      {
        "label": "B",
        "raw_label": "(b)",
        "text": "No, since there is another attesting witness who has not been summoned to\ncourt, that witness must be first examined under Section 68, Indian Evidence\nAct, 1872."
      },
      {
        "label": "C",
        "raw_label": "(C)",
        "text": "No, since one attesting witness has denied the execution, no other evidence can\nprove the execution of the Will."
      },
      {
        "label": "D",
        "raw_label": "(d)",
        "text": "Yes, since the scribe is a direct witness to the execution of the Will, and his\nevidence is admissible under Section 60, Indian Evidence Act, 1872."
      }
    ]
  },
  "after": {
    "printed_question_number": "59",
    "stem": "5 9. {

  "rule": "literal_source_boundaries_and_primary_options",
  "before": {
    "stem": "60. in terms of the time when the certificate required under Section 65b(4) of the Indian\nEvidence Act, 1872 must be produced, and specifically in the context of criminal\ntrials, the Supreme Court has held:",
    "options": [
      {
        "label": "A",
        "raw_label": "(A)",
        "text": "that the certificate must generally be produced at the time of production of\ndocuments, which would mean filing of the chargesheet in a criminal case."
      },
      {
        "label": "B",
        "raw_label": "(b)",
        "text": "that the documents, if missing, or deficient, can be supplied at a later stage\nin the trial and the court can be asked to take them on record."
      },
      {
        "label": "C",
        "raw_label": "(C)",
        "text": "that generally speaking, any application during trial to take additional\ndocuments on record must be examined as to not cause unfair prejudice to the\naccused."
      },
      {
        "label": "D",
        "raw_label": "(d)",
        "text": "All the above"
      }
    ]
  },

    "stem": "61. Partyland is a democratic republic that has a federal legislative body called the\nSenate. the Senate is the most powerful legislative body in the country, and its\ndecisions cannot be overruled by the judiciary. the Personal Party wins the general\nelections by an overwhelming majority and implements several of its policies\nthrough legislation during its term in power. in the next general elections, the Public\nParty wins an overwhelming majority at the polls and passes several legislation\nreversing the Personal Party’s changes. it also introduces new laws to implement\nits own policies. Which of the following is Waldron most likely to agree with?",
    "options": [
      {
        "label": "A",
        "raw_label": "(A)",
        "text": "Partyland is not an actual democracy"
      },
      {
        "label": "B",
        "raw_label": "(b)",
        "text": "the situation in Partyland is an illustration of the neutral model of law"
      },
      {
        "label": "C",
        "raw_label": "(C)",
        "text": "the situation in Partyland is an illustration of the partisan model of law\n("
      },
      {

        "raw_label": "d)",

    "options": [
      {
        "label": "A",
        "raw_label": "(A)",
        "text": "‘Morality of duty’ is non-obligatory."
      },
      {
        "label": "B",
        "raw_label": "(B)",
        "text": "‘Morality of duty’ is obligatory."
      },
      {
        "label": "C",
        "raw_label": "(C)",
        "text": "Rules of ‘morality of aspiration’ are a challenge to human conduct."
      },
      {
        "label": "D",
        "raw_label": "(D)",
        "text": "Human excellence is the end of ‘morality of aspiration’.\nIll. The present system of appointments as envisaged by the Constitution and as elucidated in\nthe Collegium system makes it clear that the first step is a recommendation from Collegium of\nfour senior-most judges and presided over by the Chief Justice. This process in turn requires\nwide consultation by the Chief Justice of the High Court to identify the requisite talent, so as\nto make the recommendations. Contrary to some portrayed beliefs as if this is an extremely\nsubjective system, every Chief Justice is actually required to solicit names from different\nsources whether it be sitting judges, retired judges, or prominent members of the Bar. It is\nfrom this pool of talent that he selects, after a discussion in the collegium, the most suitable\ncandidates. It is thus of utmost importance that the flow of recommendations continues for\nthe appointment process to work successfully. The current situation of vacancies, especially\nin some of the larger courts with very few recommendations in the pipeline seems to be the\ngenesis of this problem. The data placed before us, as drawn from the National Judicial Data\nGrid (NJDG) shows that five (5) High Courts alone are responsible for 54% of the pendency of\nover 57,51,312 cases i.e., the High Courts of Allahabad, Punjab & Haryana, Madras, Bombay,\nand Rajasthan. The Madras High Court has among the highest arrears in the country of 5.8 lakh\ncases despite having fewer vacancies than most other High Courts (i.e., 7%). This does not\ntake away from the requirement of appointing ad hoc Judges but supports the view that even\nif the existing vacancies are few, a situation may arise requiring the expertise of experienced\nJudges to be appointed as ad hoc Judges.\nPG"
      }
    ]

    "options": [
      {
        "label": "A",
        "raw_label": "(A)",
        "text": "‘Morality of duty’ is non-obligatory."
      },
      {
        "label": "B",
        "raw_label": "(B)",
        "text": "‘Morality of duty’ is obligatory."
      },
      {
        "label": "C",
        "raw_label": "(C)",
        "text": "Rules of ‘morality of aspiration’ are a challenge to human conduct."
      },
      {
        "label": "D",
        "raw_label": "(D)",
        "text": "Human excellence is the end of ‘morality of aspiration’. Ill. The present system of appointments as envisaged by the Constitution and as elucidated in the Collegium system makes it clear that the first step is a recommendation from Collegium of four senior-most judges and presided over by the Chief Justice. This process in turn requires wide consultation by the Chief Justice of the High Court to identify the requisite talent, so as to make the recommendations. Contrary to some portrayed beliefs as if this is an extremely subjective system, every Chief Justice is actually required to solicit names from different sources whether it be sitting judges, retired judges, or prominent members of the Bar. It is from this pool of talent that he selects, after a discussion in the collegium, the most suitable candidates. It is thus of utmost importance that the flow of recommendations continues for the appointment process to work successfully. The current situation of vacancies, especially in some of the larger courts with very few recommendations in the pipeline seems to be the genesis of this problem. The data placed before us, as drawn from the National Judicial Data Grid (NJDG) shows that five (5) High Courts alone are responsible for 54% of the pendency of over 57,51,312 cases i.e., the High Courts of Allahabad, Punjab & Haryana, Madras, Bombay, and Rajasthan. The Madras High Court has among the highest arrears in the country of 5.8 lakh cases despite having fewer vacancies than most other High Courts (i.e., 7%). This does not take away from the requirement of appointing ad hoc Judges but supports the view that even if the existing vacancies are few, a situation may arise requiring the expertise of experienced Judges to be appointed as ad hoc Judges."
      }
    ]
  },

        "text": "The assembly should be peaceful."

        "raw_label": "(C)",
        "text": "The assembly should be without arms."
      },
      {

{
  "question_id": "d3905f6d3c31af4cdf5d47d3e6380179c5fd2c8f55e489648d140783b06a0d3b:p0199:l0012:question",
  "rule": "literal_source_boundaries_and_primary_options",
  "before": {
    "stem": "28. Which of the following is not a direction given by Supreme Court of India in the judgement\nrelating to orders of maintenance and successive claims by parties in matrimonial\nproceedings?",
    "options": [
      {
        "label": "A",
        "raw_label": "(A)",
        "text": "Where successive claims for maintenance are made by a party under different\nstatutes, the Court would consider an adjustment or setoff of the amount awarded\nin previous proceedings."
      },
      {
        "label": "B",
        "raw_label": "(B)",
        "text": "Ifthe order passed in the previous proceeding/s requires modification or variation,\nany\nit would be required to be done in the same proceeding."
      },
      {
        "label": "C",
        "raw_label": "(C)",
        "text": "It is not mandatory for the applicant to disclose the previous proceeding and the\norders passed therein, in the subsequent proceeding."
      },
      {
        "label": "D",
        "raw_label": "(D)",
        "text": "The affidavit of disclosure of assets and liabilities as applicable, shall be filed by\nboth parties in all maintenance proceedings, including pending proceedings before\nany other court, as the case may be."
      }
    ]
  },
  "after": {
    "stem": "28. Which of the following is not a direction given by Supreme Court of India in the judgement relating to orders of maintenance and successive claims by parties in matrimonial proceedings?",

        "text": "Ifthe order passed in the previous proceeding/s requires modification or variation, any it would be required to be done in the same proceeding."
      },
      {

        "text": "It is not mandatory for the applicant to disclose the previous proceeding and the orders passed therein, in the subsequent proceeding."
      },

d3905f6d3c31af4cdf5d47d3e6380179c5fd2c8f55e489648d140783b06a0d3b:p0199:l0026:question
{
  "question_id": "d3905f6d3c31af4cdf5d47d3e6380179c5fd2c8f55e489648d140783b06a0d3b:p0199:l0026:question",
  "rule": "literal_source_boundaries_and_primary_options",
  "before": {
    "stem": "29. Which of the following is not correct as per Section 125 of the Code of Criminal Procedure,\n1973?",
    "options": [
      {
        "label": "A",
        "raw_label": "(A)",
        "text": "It provides for maintenance to wife/wives, illegitimate and legitimate children and\nparents."
      },
      {
        "label": "B",
        "raw_label": "(B)",
        "text": "A wife shall not be entitled to receive maintenance as per this provision from her\nhusband if she is living in adultery, or if, without any sufficient reason, she refuses\nto live with her husband, or if they are living separately by mutual consent."
      },
      {
        "label": "C",
        "raw_label": "(C)",

      },

  "before": {
    "stem": "33. based on the given excerpt, which of the following was held by the Supreme Court of\nindia in relation to the Family Courts?",
    "options": [
      {
        "label": "A",
        "raw_label": "(A)",
        "text": "Non-compliance of the prescribed mandatory procedure and infraction of principles\nof natural justice is not a technical irregularity which can be overlooked by family\ncourts."
      },
      {
        "label": "B",
        "raw_label": "(b)",
        "text": "in divorce proceedings, it is the duty of family courts to mandatorily conduct mediation\nbetween the parties."
      },

        "label": "C",
        "raw_label": "(C)",
        "text": "Non-compliance of the prescribed mandatory procedure and infraction of principles\nof natural justice is a technical irregularity which can be overlooked by family\ncourts."
      },
      {
        "label": "D",
        "raw_label": "(d)",
        "text": "Family Courts ought not to examine matters after giving due opportunity to both\nsides on their own merits and in accordance with law."
