    ],
    "stem": "42. Which of the following is correct regarding considerations in deciding issues of frustration\nof contract ?",
    "options": [
      {
        "label": "A",
        "raw_label": "(A)",
        "text": "The Doctrine of Frustration will not be applicable to assist a party that does not\nwant to fulfil its obligations under the contract."
      },
      {
        "label": "B",
        "raw_label": "(B)",
        "text": "The defence of Doctrine of Frustration is not available to a person who for the reason\nof impossibility cannot perform the contract."
      },
      {
        "label": "C",
        "raw_label": "(C)",
        "text": "Few variations from the original contract will be a defence for the parties."
      },
      {
        "label": "D",
        "raw_label": "(D)",
        "text": "The intervening event must not be entirely impossible.\nVill. The constitutional validity of the West Bengal Housing Industry Regulation Act, 2017 (WB-HIRA)\nwas Challenged on the basis that both WB-HIRA and a Parliamentary enactment, namely, the\nReal Estate (Regulation and Development) Act, 2016 (RERA) are relatable to the legislative\nsubjects contained in Entries 6 and 7 of List Ill (Concurrent List) of the Seventh Schedule\nof the Constitution of India. WB-HIRA has neither been reserved for nor has it received\nPresidential assent under Article 254(2) of the Constitution of India, which was necessary\nsince it was going to occupy the same field as the RERA, a law which had been enacted by\nthe Parliament. The State enactment contains certain provisions which are either: directly\ninconsistent with the corresponding provisions of the Central enactment; a virtual replica of\nor\nthe Central enactment; and Parliament having legislated on a field covered by the Concurrent\nList, it is constitutionally impermissible for the State Legislature to enact a law over the same\nsubject matter by setting up a parallel legislation. The analysis indicates repugnancy between\nWB-HIRA and RERA. Undoubtedly, as Article 254(1) postulates, the legislation enacted by\nthe State legislature is void ‘to the extent of the repugnancy’. There is, not only a direct conflict\nof certain provisions between the RERA and WB-HIRA, but there is also a failure of the State\nlegislature to incorporate statutory safeguards in WB-HIRA, which have been introduced in\nthe RERA for protecting the interest of the purchasers of real estate. For repugnancy under\nArticle 254 of the Constitution, there is a twin requirement to be fulfilled: firstly, there has to be\na ‘repugnancy’ between a Central and State Act; and secondly, the Presidential assent has\nto be held as being non-existent. The test for determining such repugnancy is indeed to find\nout the dominant intention of both the legislations and whether such dominant intentions of\nboth the legislations are alike or different. A provision in one legislation in order to give effect\nto its dominant purpose may incidentally be on the same subject as covered by the provision\nof the other legislation, but such partial incidental of the in a different\nor coverage same area\ncontext and to achieve a different purpose does not attract the doctrine of repugnancy. In\norder to attract the doctrine of repugnancy, both the legislations must be substantially on the\nsame subject. Hence, WB-HIRA is repugnant to the RERA, and is hence unconstitutional.\nM 14\nPG"
      }
    ]
  },

        "text": "The intervening event must not be entirely impossible. Vill. The constitutional validity of the West Bengal Housing Industry Regulation Act, 2017 (WB-HIRA) was Challenged on the basis that both WB-HIRA and a Parliamentary enactment, namely, the Real Estate (Regulation and Development) Act, 2016 (RERA) are relatable to the legislative subjects contained in Entries 6 and 7 of List Ill (Concurrent List) of the Seventh Schedule of the Constitution of India. WB-HIRA has neither been reserved for nor has it received Presidential assent under Article 254(2) of the Constitution of India, which was necessary since it was going to occupy the same field as the RERA, a law which had been enacted by the Parliament. The State enactment contains certain provisions which are either: directly inconsistent with the corresponding provisions of the Central enactment; a virtual replica of or the Central enactment; and Parliament having legislated on a field covered by the Concurrent List, it is constitutionally impermissible for the State Legislature to enact a law over the same subject matter by setting up a parallel legislation. The analysis indicates repugnancy between WB-HIRA and RERA. Undoubtedly, as Article 254(1) postulates, the legislation enacted by the State legislature is void ‘to the extent of the repugnancy’. There is, not only a direct conflict of certain provisions between the RERA and WB-HIRA, but there is also a failure of the State legislature to incorporate statutory safeguards in WB-HIRA, which have been introduced in the RERA for protecting the interest of the purchasers of real estate. For repugnancy under Article 254 of the Constitution, there is a twin requirement to be fulfilled: firstly, there has to be a ‘repugnancy’ between a Central and State Act; and secondly, the Presidential assent has to be held as being non-existent. The test for determining such repugnancy is indeed to find out the dominant intention of both the legislations and whether such dominant intentions of both the legislations are alike or different. A provision in one legislation in order to give effect to its dominant purpose may incidentally be on the same subject as covered by the provision of the other legislation, but such partial incidental of the in a different or coverage same area context and to achieve a different purpose does not attract the doctrine of repugnancy. In order to attract the doctrine of repugnancy, both the legislations must be substantially on the same subject. Hence, WB-HIRA is repugnant to the RERA, and is hence unconstitutional. M 14"
      }
    ]
  },

  "before": {
    "stem": "98. ‘A’ is accused of having committed an offence on January 1, 2022. He attained the\nage of 16 on March 31, 2022. On the date of hearing, he claimed that on the date of\ncommission of the offence, he was a child. Which of the following statement is true?",

        "text": "For raising the plea of juvenility, the age on the date of trial is considered and not\nthe age on the date of commission of offence."

d3905f6d3c31af4cdf5d47d3e6380179c5fd2c8f55e489648d140783b06a0d3b:p0437:l0025:question
{
  "question_id": "d3905f6d3c31af4cdf5d47d3e6380179c5fd2c8f55e489648d140783b06a0d3b:p0437:l0025:question",
  "rule": "literal_source_boundaries_and_primary_options",
  "before": {
    "section_id": "unknown",
    "stem": "20. Which of the following statements is incorrect in view of the judgment in Pramati\nEducational and Cultural Trust v. Union of India (2014) 8 SCC 1?",
    "options": [
      {
        "label": "A",
        "raw_label": "A.",
        "text": "Article 15(5) does not violate the freedom of private unaided educational\ninstitutions under Article 19(1)(g) of the Constitution."
      },
      {
        "label": "B",
        "raw_label": "B.",
        "text": "Articles 15(5) and 21A do not alter the basic structure of the Constitution and are\nconstitutionally valid."
      },
      {
        "label": "C",

    "stem": "25. Which of the following reasons led to the setting aside of the practice of ‘talaq-e-\nbiddat’, triple talaq in Shayara Bano v. d3905f6d3c31af4cdf5d47d3e6380179c5fd2c8f55e489648d140783b06a0d3b:p0439:l0017:question
{
  "question_id": "d3905f6d3c31af4cdf5d47d3e6380179c5fd2c8f55e489648d140783b06a0d3b:p0439:l0017:question",
  "rule": "literal_source_boundaries_and_primary_options",
  "before": {
    "section_id": "unknown",
    "stem": "26. Which is the correct position in law on an Ordinance promulgated under Article 123 of\nthe Constitution of India, following the judgment in Krishna Kumar v. State of Bihar\n(2017) 3 SCC 1?\n(i) Power conferred upon the President under Article 123 is legislative in character\nand the satisfaction of the President is immune from judicial review.\n(ii) An Ordinance promulgated under Article 123 must be laid before the\nParliament, which is a mandatory constitutional obligation cast upon the\ngovernment.\n(iii) An Ordinance promulgated in exercise of powers under Article 213 cannot\ncreate enduring rights in favour of individuals\n(iv) Re-promulgation of an Ordinance is a fraud on the Constitution.\nChoose the correct answer from the following:"
  },
  "after": {
    "section_id": "source-numbering-block@p0433:l0001",
    "stem": "26. Which is the correct position in law on an Ordinance promulgated under Article 123 of the Constitution of India, following the judgment in Krishna Kumar v. State of Bihar (2017) 3 SCC 1? (i) Power conferred upon the President under Article 123 is legislative in character and the satisfaction of the President is immune from judicial review. (ii) An Ordinance promulgated under Article 123 must be laid before the Parliament, which is a mandatory constitutional obligation cast upon the government. (iii) An Ordinance promulgated in exercise of powers under Article 213 cannot create enduring rights in favour of individuals (iv) Re-promulgation of an Ordinance is a fraud on the Constitution. Choose the correct answer from the following:"
  },

{

  "before": {
    "section_id": "unknown",
    "options": [
      {
        "label": "A",
        "raw_label": "A.",
        "text": "The Jammu and Kashmir Code of Criminal Procedure has no provision for\ntransfer of a case from a Court in Jammu and Kashmir to any Court outside that\nState and, therefore, no criminal case can be transferred from the State of\nJammu and Kashmir to any other Court outside that State."
      },
      {
        "label": "B",
        "raw_label": "B.",
        "text": "Article 370 of the Constitution of India confers merely a “Temporary” status on\nthe State of Jammu and Kashmir."
      },
      {
        "label": "C",
        "raw_label": "C.",
        "text": "Article 371-D and Presidential Orders issued thereunder override any other\nprovision of the Constitution of India."
      },
      {
        "label": "D",
        "raw_label": "D.",
        "text": "The citizens of India have a fundamental right to reside and settle in any part of\nIndia except the State of Jammu and Kashmir."
      }
    ]
  },

d3905f6d3c31af4cdf5d47d3e6380179c5fd2c8f55e489648d140783b06a0d3b:p0459:l0000:question
{
  "question_id": "d3905f6d3c31af4cdf5d47d3e6380179c5fd2c8f55e489648d140783b06a0d3b:p0459:l0000:question",
  "rule": "literal_source_boundaries_and_primary_options",
  "before": {
    "section_id": "unknown",
    "stem": "23. A, from Kerala, writes a letter to B who lives in Delhi requesting the supply of certain goods\nat a certain price. While accepting the offer by writing a letter on his printed letterhead B\nwrites at the top of the letterhead, \"Subject to the jurisdiction of Delhi Courts.\" Later a\ndispute arises and A files an action in Kerala.",
    "options": [
      {
        "label": "A",
        "raw_label": "A.",
        "text": "A cannot file legal proceedings in Kerala since B has clearly indicated that\nthe jurisdiction is restricted to Delhi courts."
      },
      {
        "label": "B",
        "raw_label": "B.",
        "text": "The agreement is void as it tends to defeat the legal process."
      },
      {
        "label": "C",
        "raw_label": "C.",
        "text": "Since B has written the words at the top of his letterhead, they do not\nbecome part of the contract and hence A is free to file the action in any\ncourt which has jurisdiction."
      },
      {
        "label": "D",
        "raw_label": "D.",
        "text": "Since the letterhead is part of the agreement of acceptance, the agreement\nis enforceable."
      }
    ]
  },
  "after": {

d3905f6d3c31af4cdf5d47d3e6380179c5fd2c8f55e489648d140783b06a0d3b:p0459:l0026:question
{
  "question_id": "d3905f6d3c31af4cdf5d47d3e6380179c5fd2c8f55e489648d140783b06a0d3b:p0459:l0026:question",
  "rule": "literal_source_boundaries_and_primary_options",
  "before": {
    "section_id": "unknown",
    "stem": "26. A transport company issued a circular to all its drivers that they should not compete or\nobstruct other buses plying in the route. Driver A, in contravention of the express\nprohibition, obstructed another bus and while doing so met with an accident in which B was\ninjured.",
    "options": [
      {
        "label": "A",
        "raw_label": "A.",
        "text": "The company is not liable as it had expressly prohibited the drivers from\ncompeting and obstructing other buses."
      },
      {
        "label": "B",
        "raw_label": "B.",
        "text": "The company is liable as the accident happened in the course of\nemployment."
      },
      {
        "label": "C",
        "raw_label": "C.",
        "text": "The company is not liable because the driver had disobeyed the company's\ninstructions and thereby acted outside the course of employment."
      },
      {
        "label": "D",
        "raw_label": "D.",
        "text": "The company is not liable because the driver had not acted for the benefit\nof the employer, the company."
      }
    ]
  },

d3905f6d3c31af4cdf5d47d3e6380179c5fd2c8f55e489648d140783b06a0d3b:p0460:l0004:question
{
  "question_id": "d3905f6d3c31af4cdf5d47d3e6380179c5fd2c8f55e489648d140783b06a0d3b:p0460:l0004:question",
  "rule": "literal_source_boundaries_and_primary_options",
  "before": {
    "section_id": "unknown",
    "stem": "27. A was riding his bicycle on a rainy day on a road which had no street lights. He came in\ncontact with a live wire lying on the road which was inundated with water and got\nelectrocuted. A's wife brought an action against the Electricity Board for negligence.",
    "options": [
      {
        "label": "A",
        "raw_label": "A.",
        "text": "The Board is not liable as the accident happened because of the negligence\nof the cyclist."
      },
      {
        "label": "B",
        "raw_label": "B.",
        "text": "The Board is not liable as the accident happened because of the negligence\nof a third party, as the Board argued that a third party tried to siphon off\nthe electricity illegally, and negligently left the wire on the road."
      },
      {
        "label": "C",
        "raw_label": "C.",
        "text": "The Board is not liable because of the rain and storm, and as such, it was an\nAct of God."
      },
      {
        "label": "D",
        "raw_label": "D.",
        "text": "The Board is liable as supplying electricity is an inherently dangerous act,\nand as such, the Board is absolutely liable."
      }
    ]
  },
  "after": {
    "section_id": "source-numbering-block@p0454:l0001",

d3905f6d3c31af4cdf5d47d3e6380179c5fd2c8f55e489648d140783b06a0d3b:p0460:l0016:question
{
  "question_id": "d3905f6d3c31af4cdf5d47d3e6380179c5fd2c8f55e489648d140783b06a0d3b:p0460:l0016:question",
  "rule": "literal_source_boundaries_and_primary_options",
  "before": {
    "section_id": "unknown",
    "stem": "28. The Supreme Court in Indian Medical Association v. V P Shanta, (1995) 6 SCC 651, has held\nthat:",
    "options": [
      {
        "label": "A",
        "raw_label": "A.",
        "text": "a hospital rendering free service to some patients and paid services to\nothers is not covered under the definition of service under the Consumer\nProtection Act, as gratuitous services is excluded from the definition of\nservice under the Act."
      },
      {
        "label": "B",
        "raw_label": "B.",
        "text": "a hospital which renders service to the patients is covered under the\nConsumer Protection Act whether they are rendering a contract of service\nor contract for service."
      },
      {
        "label": "C",
        "raw_label": "C.",
        "text": "a hospital which is run by the government is not covered under the\nConsumer Protection Act and the patient who suffers due to the negligence\nof a doctor working in the hospital will have to file the case in a civil court\nunder the law of tort."
      },
      {
        "label": "D",
        "raw_label": "D.",
        "text": "a hospital which renders free service to some patients and paid service to\nsome others is covered under the definition of service, as the patients\nwho receive free service are the beneficiaries of the service hired by the\npatients who pay for the service."
      }
    ]
  },
  "after": {
